cues.text: Born Into Rejection
Born in Lima, Peru, on 9 December 1579, Martin de Porres was the illegitimate son of a Spanish nobleman, Juan de Porres, and Ana Velázquez, a freed slave woman of African descent.
His father, disturbed by his son's dark complexion, refused for years to acknowledge Martin as his own, abandoning mother and son to a childhood marked by real poverty.
This rejection was rooted entirely in the racial prejudice of colonial Peruvian society, and Martin carried it without recorded bitterness for the rest of his life.
After only two years of primary schooling, he was apprenticed instead to a barber-surgeon, where he learned both a practical trade and the rudimentary medical arts of his day.
Barred by His Order's Own Law

Apprenticed as a boy to a barber-surgeon, where he learned the rudiments of medicine alongside his trade, Martin at fifteen sought admission to the Dominican priory of the Holy Rosary in Lima, drawn to a life of religious service.
The Dominican constitution of the era, however, explicitly barred men of African or mixed-race descent from full membership in the order.
Martin therefore offered himself as a servant, performing the community's most menial labor without complaint or any expectation of eventual advancement.
A Rule Quietly Set Aside
Martin's evident holiness, humility, and skill in caring for the sick gradually won over even those brothers who had initially mocked him for his ancestry.
After eight years of faithful, uncomplaining service, the prior, Juan de Lorenzana, permitted Martin to profess vows as a Dominican lay brother in 1603.
He quietly set aside the order's own racial restriction rather than continue excluding a man whose sanctity had by then become impossible to ignore.
A Healer for the Whole City
Placed in charge of the priory's infirmary, Martin became renowned throughout Lima for his tireless, tender care of the sick.
He extended his ministry well beyond his own community's walls to the city's poor, enslaved Africans, and abandoned children alike.
He treated Spanish nobles and destitute slaves with precisely the same careful attention.
He established an orphanage and a children's hospital, funded by alms he tirelessly solicited from Lima's wealthier citizens.
Contemporaries credited him with numerous miraculous cures, alongside more extraordinary reported phenomena including bilocation and an unusual, gentle rapport with animals.
This rapport is still recalled in the broom and small creatures that accompany his image in art.
Friendship Among Lima's Saints

Martin formed a close and mutually supportive friendship with two other future saints of colonial Lima — St. Rose of Lima , who deeply respected his penances and his labors, and St. Juan Macías , a fellow Dominican lay brother.

Together, the three formed an extraordinary concentration of holiness within a single generation of one relatively small colonial city, each drawing quiet encouragement from the others' shared, hidden austerity.
Legacy

Martin fell seriously ill in January 1639 and endured nearly a year of painful sickness before dying on 3 November 1639, at nearly sixty years old; the city's viceroy himself, tradition holds, knelt beside his deathbed seeking his blessing.
When his tomb was opened twenty-five years later, witnesses reported his body found still intact and exhaling a remarkable fragrance.
Beatified in 1837 and canonized in 1962 by Pope John XXIII, Martin de Porres remains patron of racial harmony, mixed-race people, and all who work for interracial reconciliation.

Once formally excluded from full membership in his own religious community by the color of his skin, he became, through patient, uncomplaining service, one of the most universally beloved saints the whole of Latin America has ever produced.
His example continues to be invoked wherever the Church prays for an end to the very prejudice that once, quite literally, barred him from her altar.
